Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 78, verse 1–5:

Surat (ʿAmma) is Meccan, and it is also called Surat (al-Naba'). It has forty or forty-one verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿About what do they question one another? About the tremendous news, about which they are in disagreement. No! They will soon know. Then, no! They will soon know.﴾

Allah's words: ﴿ʿAmma yatasaʾalun?﴾ ʿAmma is an interrogative particle, and for this reason the alif of (ma) is dropped from it, so that the statement is distinguished from the question. The same applies to (fimma and mimma) when you are asking. The meaning is: about what do some of them question one another? Al-Zajjaj said: the original form is ʿan ma, and the nun was assimilated into the mim because they share the nasal quality (ghunna). The pronoun in yatasaʾalun refers to the Quraysh. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the Qur'an was revealed, the Quraysh would sit and talk among themselves; some of them affirmed it and some of them denied it, so (ʿAmma yatasaʾalun?) was revealed. It has also been said that ʿamma means "fima" (about what): the polytheists dispute and quarrel about what?

Allah's words: ﴿ʿan al-naba' al-ʿazim﴾ means: they question one another about the tremendous news. The word ʿan is not connected to the yatasaʾalun that appears in the recitation, because that would require the interrogative particle to enter it, so that it would read "ʿan al-naba' al-ʿazim" like your saying: "How much is your money, thirty or forty?" For the reason we have mentioned, it is impossible for it to be connected to the yatasaʾalun in the recitation; rather it is connected to another, implied verb. This is permissible because yatasaʾalun precedes it; this was said by al-Mahdawi. Some scholars have mentioned that the interrogative in His words "ʿan" is repeated but implied, as if he said: "About what do they question one another? About the tremendous news?" According to this, it is connected to the first verse. Al-Naba' al-ʿazim means the great report.

﴿Alladhi hum fihi mukhtalifun﴾ means: some of them differ with one another about it, so one affirms and another denies. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: It is the Qur'an. The proof is His words: "Say: It is a tremendous news, from which you turn away." So the Qur'an is news, information and narrative, and it is news of tremendous importance. Sa'id related from Qatadah, who said: It is the resurrection after death; people became two groups concerning it: one affirming and one denying. It has also been said: it is the command of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: That is because the Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about many things, and Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed him of their disagreement; then He threatened them, saying: "No! They will soon know," that is, they will soon know the outcome of the Qur'an, or they will soon know the resurrection: is it true or false? "No" is a rebuttal of their denial of the resurrection or their denial of the Qur'an, and it is therefore pausing on it. It may also be in the sense of "truly" or "ألا" (indeed), in which case one begins with it. The more apparent view is that their questioning was only about the resurrection. Some of our scholars said: What indicates this is His words, mighty and majestic: "Indeed the Day of Decision is an appointed time" (78:17), which shows that they were questioning one another about the resurrection.

﴿Then, no! They will soon know﴾ means: truly, they will certainly know the truth of what Muhammad ﷺ brought of the Qur'an and of what he told them about resurrection after death. Al-Dahhak said: "No! They will soon know" refers to the disbelievers, the outcome of their denial; "Then, no! They will soon know" refers to the believers, the outcome of their affirmation. It has also been said the reverse. Al-Hasan said: this is a threat after a threat. The common reading of both is with the yaʾ, as a report, in accordance with His words yatasaʾalun and His words "fihi mukhtalifun." Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Malik ibn Dinar read both with the taʾ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾ He points them to His power over resurrection. That is: Our power to bring these things into existence is greater than Our power to bring them back. Al-mihad means the spread-out bed and the couch. Exalted is He has said: ﴿He who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:22]. It is also read as mahdan (a cradle). Its meaning is that it is for them like a cradle for an infant, which is what is prepared for him so that he is laid down upon it. (And the mountains as pegs) That is, so that it may remain steady, not sway, and not tilt with its people.

(And We created you in pairs) That is, kinds: male and female. It was also said: colours. It was also said: every pair of ugly and beautiful, tall and short, so that conditions differ and reflection occurs, so the one who is favoured gives thanks and the one who is less favoured is patient.

(And We made your sleep) "Made" means "set," and for this reason it takes two objects. Subatan (rest) is the second object, meaning repose for your bodies. From this comes the name Saturday (al-sabt), meaning the day of rest. It was said to the Children of Israel: rest on this day and do no work in it. Ibn al-Anbari rejected this and said: subat is not said of rest. It was also said: its origin is stretching out. It is said: the woman "sabatat" her hair when she loosened and released it, so subat is like extension, and a man "masbut al-khalq" means stretched out. When a man wishes to rest, he stretches out, so rest was called sabt.

It was also said: its origin is cutting off. It is said: "sabata sha'rahu sabtan," meaning he shaved his hair. As though, when one sleeps, he is cut off from people and from occupation. So subat resembles death, except that the soul has not departed from it. It is also said: "sayr sabt," meaning an easy, smooth journey. The poet said: [Hamid ibn Thawr: "The sabt is swift travel. The dhamil is lazy travel."]

And a she-camel with stretched flanks: by day its travel is sabt, and by night its pace is dhamil.

(And We made the night a garment) That is, its darkness clothes you and covers you. This is what al-Tabari said. Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: that is, a resting place for you.

(And We made the day for livelihood) There is an ellipsis here, meaning a time for livelihood: a time of going about to seek livelihood. Livelihood is everything one lives by, such as food, drink and other things. On this reading, ma'shan (livelihood) is a noun of time, so that the second is the first. It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning living, with the omission of a modifier.

(And We built above you seven strong) That is, seven heavens, made firm: well-fashioned in creation and firmly constructed.

(And We made a blazing lamp) That is, a blazing flame, and it is the sun. Here "made" means "created," because it takes one object. Wahhaj means that which has heat: it is said: "wahija yahij wahjan, wahajan, wahajanan." It is said of a gem when it shines: it "tawahhaja." Ibn Abbas said: wahhajan means shining, glittering.

(And We sent down from the rain-bearing clouds abundant water) Mujahid and Qatadah said: al-mu'sirat are the winds. Ibn Abbas also said this: as though they squeeze the clouds. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that they are the clouds. Sufyan, al-Rabi', Abu al-Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: they are the clouds that are squeezed with water and have not yet rained, like the girl who is approaching menstruation and has not yet menstruated. Abu al-Najm said: [She walks gently, her veil slipping; she has reached the age of 'i'sar' or her 'i'sar' is near.]

[This addition from Abu Hayyan is supported by the agreement of the manuscripts of the original on mentioning Abu al-Najm.]

And another said: [Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah: "My shield, against whom I was guarding, were three figures: two maidens and one who is nearly grown."]

And [Al-Ba'ith, as in al-Lisan, whose version of the verse is: "And one with a bright glow like the daisy, the fading of the breeze and the laden clouds." Al-dawalih are clouds weighed down with water, and al-dhihab with a kasra on the dhal means weak rains.] another said:

"And one with a glow like the daisy, adorned by the fading breeze and the light clouds."

So winds are called mu'sirat. It is said: "a'sarat al-rih tu'sir i'sara," when it stirs up dust, and this is al-i'sar. Clouds are also called mu'sirat because they rain. Qatadah also said: al-mu'sirat is the sky. Al-Nahhas said: these sayings are sound. The winds that bring rain are called mu'sirat, and the winds fertilise the clouds, so rain occurs, and in this sense rain falls from the wind. It is possible that the sayings are one, and the meaning is: and We sent down from the winds' bearers, the mu'sirat, abundant water. The most sound saying is that al-mu'sirat are the clouds, since it is well known that rain comes from them. Had it been "bil-mu'sirat," the wind would have been more fitting. In al-Sihah: al-mu'sirat are clouds that squeeze out rain. "U'sira al-qawm" means they were rained upon, and from this someone read "wa-fihi ya'sirun" [Yusuf 12:49]. Al-mu'sir is a girl when she first reaches puberty and menstruates; it is said: "qad a'sarat," as though she has entered or reached the age of her youth. The rajaz poet said: [Mansur ibn Mardad al-Asadi: "A girl in Safwan, her home, walking gently, her veil slipping. She has reached puberty, or her time of puberty is near."]

Its plural is ma'asir. It is said: it is the one near menstruation, because i'sar in a girl is like adolescence in a boy. I heard this from Abu al-Ghawth al-A'rabi. Another said: al-mu'sir is a cloud that is due to rain. It is said: "ajanna al-zar'u fa-huwa mujinn," meaning the crop has come to the point of ripening, and likewise a cloud when it is about to rain has "a'sara." Al-Mubarrad said: one says "sahab mu'sir," meaning holding water, from which water is squeezed out little by little. From this comes al-'asar, with a fatha on the ayn, meaning a refuge one turns to, and al-'usra with a damma, also meaning refuge. This meaning has already passed in the surah of Yusuf [see vol. 9, p. 205], and praise belongs to God. Abu Zubayd said: [He said this in lament for his sister's son, who died of thirst on the road to Makkah.]: "Thirsty, seeking help, and none helps him, and he had been a refuge for the one who was saved."

From this comes al-mu'sir for a girl who is close to puberty; she is called mu'sir because she is kept in the house, so the house becomes her 'asr (enclosure).

In the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah: "wa-anzalna bil-mu'sirat." But what is in the codices is "min al-mu'sirat." It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning living, with the omission of a modifier.

(And We built above you seven strong) That is, seven heavens, made firm: well-fashioned in creation and firmly constructed.

(And We made a blazing lamp) That is, a blazing flame, and it is the sun. Here "made" means "created," because it takes one object. Wahhaj means that which has heat: it is said: "wahija yahij wahjan, wahajan, wahajanan." It is said of a gem when it shines: it "tawahhaja." Ibn Abbas said: wahhajan means shining, glittering.

(And We sent down from the rain-bearing clouds abundant water) Mujahid and Qatadah said: al-mu'sirat are the winds. Ibn Abbas also said this: as though they squeeze the clouds. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that they are the clouds. Sufyan, al-Rabi', Abu al-Aliyah and al-Dahhak said: they are the clouds that are squeezed with water and have not yet rained, like the girl who is approaching menstruation and has not yet menstruated. Abu al-Najm said: [She walks gently, her veil slipping; she has reached the age of 'i'sar' or her 'i'sar' is near.]

[This addition from Abu Hayyan is supported by the agreement of the manuscripts of the original on mentioning Abu al-Najm.]

And another said: [Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah: "My shield, against whom I was guarding, were three figures: two maidens and one who is nearly grown."]

And [Al-Ba'ith, as in al-Lisan, whose version of the verse is: "And one with a bright glow like the daisy, the fading of the breeze and the laden clouds." Al-dawalih are clouds weighed down with water, and al-dhihab with a kasra on the dhal means weak rains.] another said:

"And one with a glow like the daisy, adorned by the fading breeze and the light clouds."

So winds are called mu'sirat. It is said: "a'sarat al-rih tu'sir i'sara," when it stirs up dust, and this is al-i'sar. Clouds are also called mu'sirat because they rain. Qatadah also said: al-mu'sirat is the sky. Al-Nahhas said: these sayings are sound. The winds that bring rain are called mu'sirat, and the winds fertilise the clouds, so rain occurs, and in this sense rain falls from the wind. It is possible that the sayings are one, and the meaning is: and We sent down from the winds' bearers, the mu'sirat, abundant water. The most sound saying is that al-mu'sirat are the clouds, since it is well known that rain comes from them. Had it been "bil-mu'sirat," the wind would have been more fitting. In al-Sihah: al-mu'sirat are clouds that squeeze out rain. "U'sira al-qawm" means they were rained upon, and from this someone read "wa-fihi ya'sirun" [Yusuf 12:49]. Al-mu'sir is a girl when she first reaches puberty and menstruates; it is said: "qad a'sarat," as though she has entered or reached the age of her youth. The rajaz poet said: [Mansur ibn Mardad al-Asadi: "A girl in Safwan, her home, walking gently, her veil slipping. She has reached puberty, or her time of puberty is near."]

Its plural is ma'asir. It is said: it is the one near menstruation, because i'sar in a girl is like adolescence in a boy. I heard this from Abu al-Ghawth al-A'rabi. Another said: al-mu'sir is a cloud that is due to rain. It is said: "ajanna al-zar'u fa-huwa mujinn," meaning the crop has come to the point of ripening, and likewise a cloud when it is about to rain has "a'sara." Al-Mubarrad said: one says "sahab mu'sir," meaning holding water, from which water is squeezed out little by little. From this comes al-'asar, with a fatha on the ayn, meaning a refuge one turns to, and al-'usra with a damma, also meaning refuge. This meaning has already passed in the surah of Yusuf [see vol. 9, p. 205], and praise belongs to God. Abu Zubayd said: [He said this in lament for his sister's son, who died of thirst on the road to Makkah.]: "Thirsty, seeking help, and none helps him, and he had been a refuge for the one who was saved."

From this comes al-mu'sir for a girl who is close to puberty; she is called mu'sir because she is kept in the house, so the house becomes her 'asr (enclosure).

In the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah: "wa-anzalna bil-mu'sirat." But what is in the codices is "min al-mu'sirat." Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "min al-mu'sirat," that is, from the heavens. (Abundant water) pouring forth, continuous, from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others. It is said: "thajajtu dammahu fa-ana athujjuhu thajjan," I poured out his blood, and "qad thajja al-dam yathujj thuiujan," the blood flowed, and likewise water. It is intransitive and transitive. Al-thajjaj in the verse means that which pours out. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, pouring, and it is transitive, as if it pours out itself, that is, pours. Ubayd ibn al-Abras said: [The verse describes rain; munsah means split with water. In the diwan: "fa-tharraj a'laahu."]:

"Its upper part poured out, then its lower part shook, and it was constrained by the burden of water, split open."

In a hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ), he was asked about the accepted pilgrimage (al-hajj al-mabrur), and he said: [al-'ajj wa-al-thajj]. Al-'ajj is raising the voice in the talbiyah, and al-thajj is shedding blood and slaughtering sacrificial animals. Ibn Zayd said: thajjajan means abundant. The meaning is one.

His saying, Exalted is He: (That We may bring forth thereby) That is, by that water, grain such as wheat, barley and other things; and plants of (al-abb), which is what animals eat of grass; and (gardens) that is, orchards; (thick-entwined) that is, intertwined with one another because their branches are interlaced, and it has no singular, like al-awza' and al-akhyaf. It was also said: the singular of al-alfaf is lif with a kasra, and luff with a damma. Al-Kisai mentioned this and said:

"A garden thick with growth, and a plentiful life, and companions all white and bright."

And also from him and from Abu 'Ubaydah: lafif, like sharif and ashraf. It was also said: it is a plural of plural, related by al-Kisai. It was also said: the sense is: and We bring forth with it gardens thick-entwined, and the phrase is elided because the context indicates it. Then this entwining and joining means that the trees in the orchards are close together, so the branches of each tree are close because of their strength.

That is: Our power to bring these things into existence is greater than Our power to bring them back. Al-mihad means the spread-out bed and the couch. Exalted is He has said: ﴿He who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:22]. It is also read as mahdan (a cradle). Its meaning is that it is for them like a cradle for an infant, which is what is prepared for him so that he is laid down upon it. (And the mountains as pegs) That is, so that it may remain steady, not sway, and not tilt with its people.

(And We created you in pairs) That is, kinds: male and female. It was also said: colours. It was also said: every pair of ugly and beautiful, tall and short, so that conditions differ and reflection occurs, so the one who is favoured gives thanks and the one who is less favoured is patient.

It is said: the woman "sabatat" her hair when she loosened and released it, so subat is like extension, and a man "masbut al-khalq" means stretched out. When a man wishes to rest, he stretches out, so rest was called sabt.

It was also said: its origin is cutting off. It is said: "sabata sha'rahu sabtan," meaning he shaved his hair. As though, when one sleeps, he is cut off from people and from occupation. The dhamil is lazy travel."]

And a she-camel with stretched flanks: by day its travel is sabt, and by night its pace is dhamil.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 78, verse 17–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is an appointed time﴾ meaning a time, a gathering place, and a appointed meeting for the first and the last, because of what Allah promised of recompense and reward. It is called the Day of Judgment (yawm al-fasl) because Allah, Exalted is He, will decide therein between His creatures.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾, meaning for the Resurrection, ﴿you will come forth﴾, meaning to the place of gathering, ﴿in multitudes﴾, meaning in nations, each nation with its leader. It is also said: in groups and companies. The singular is fawj. The word yawman is in the accusative as a substitute for the first yawm.

It is narrated from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal: I said, "O Messenger of Allah! Tell me about the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: 'The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.'" The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Mu'adh ibn Jabal, you have asked about a tremendous matter." Then he let his eyes shed tears, and then he said: "Ten categories of my ummah will be gathered scattered, Allah having distinguished them from the congregations of the Muslims and changed their forms. Among them are those in the form of monkeys, some in the form of pigs, some upside down, their feet above them and their faces dragged upon them, some blind wandering about, some deaf and mute who do not understand, some who chew their tongues, which hang down upon their chests, pus flowing from their mouths as saliva, which the people of the gathering find loathsome, some whose hands and feet are cut off, some crucified on trunks of fire, some whose stench is worse than carrion, and some who wear flowing garments of tar clinging to their skins. As for those in the form of monkeys, they are the tale-bearers among the people, that is, the gossipers. As for those in the form of pigs, they are the people of illicit gain, the forbidden, and the unjust tolls. As for those who are upside down with their heads and faces, they are the consumers of usury. The blind are those who act unjustly in judgment. The deaf and mute are those who are impressed by their own deeds. Those who chew their tongues are the scholars and storytellers whose speech contradicts their actions. Those whose hands and feet are cut off are those who harm their neighbours. Those crucified on trunks of fire are those who inform on people to the ruler. Those whose stench is worse than carrion are those who indulge in desires and pleasures and withhold the right of Allah from their wealth. As for those who wear the garments, they are the people of arrogance, pride and vanity."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the heaven is opened and becomes gates﴾, meaning for the descent of the angels, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the day the heaven will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾ [Al-Furqan: 25]. It is also said: it will be torn apart and become fragments like gates, so the accusative of "gates" in this interpretation is by omission of the particle "ka" (like). It is also said: the estimate is "and it becomes possessing gates," because all of it will become gates. It is also said: its gates are its paths. It is also said: it will dissolve and scatter until gates appear in it. It is also said: every servant has two gates in the heaven: a gate for his deeds and a gate for his provision, and when the Resurrection comes, the gates will be opened.

In the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then we were taken up to the heaven, and Jibril asked for it to be opened. It was said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad.' It was said: 'Has he been sent for?' He said: 'He has been sent for.' So it was opened for us."

﴿And the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾, meaning they become nothing, just as a mirage: the onlooker thinks it is water, and it is not water. It is also said: they are set in motion, meaning they are uprooted from their foundations. It is also said: they are removed from their places.

In the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then we were taken up to the heaven, and Jibril asked for it to be opened. It was said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad.' It was said: 'Has he been sent for?' He said: 'He has been sent for.' So it was opened for us."

﴿And the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾, meaning they become nothing, just as a mirage: the onlooker thinks it is water, and it is not water. It is also said: they are set in motion, meaning they are uprooted from their foundations. It is also said: they are removed from their places.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 78, verse 17–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is an appointed time﴾ meaning a time, a gathering place, and a appointed meeting for the first and the last, because of what Allah promised of recompense and reward. It is called the Day of Judgment (yawm al-fasl) because Allah, Exalted is He, will decide therein between His creatures.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾, meaning for the Resurrection, ﴿you will come forth﴾, meaning to the place of gathering, ﴿in multitudes﴾, meaning in nations, each nation with its leader. It is also said: in groups and companies. The singular is fawj. The word yawman is in the accusative as a substitute for the first yawm.

It is narrated from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal: I said, "O Messenger of Allah! Tell me about the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: 'The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.'" The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Mu'adh ibn Jabal, you have asked about a tremendous matter." Then he let his eyes shed tears, and then he said: "Ten categories of my ummah will be gathered scattered, Allah having distinguished them from the congregations of the Muslims and changed their forms. Among them are those in the form of monkeys, some in the form of pigs, some upside down, their feet above them and their faces dragged upon them, some blind wandering about, some deaf and mute who do not understand, some who chew their tongues, which hang down upon their chests, pus flowing from their mouths as saliva, which the people of the gathering find loathsome, some whose hands and feet are cut off, some crucified on trunks of fire, some whose stench is worse than carrion, and some who wear flowing garments of tar clinging to their skins. As for those in the form of monkeys, they are the tale-bearers among the people, that is, the gossipers. As for those in the form of pigs, they are the people of illicit gain, the forbidden, and the unjust tolls. As for those who are upside down with their heads and faces, they are the consumers of usury. The blind are those who act unjustly in judgment. The deaf and mute are those who are impressed by their own deeds. Those who chew their tongues are the scholars and storytellers whose speech contradicts their actions. Those whose hands and feet are cut off are those who harm their neighbours. Those crucified on trunks of fire are those who inform on people to the ruler. Those whose stench is worse than carrion are those who indulge in desires and pleasures and withhold the right of Allah from their wealth. As for those who wear the garments, they are the people of arrogance, pride and vanity."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the heaven is opened and becomes gates﴾, meaning for the descent of the angels, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the day the heaven will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾ [Al-Furqan: 25]. It is also said: it will be torn apart and become fragments like gates, so the accusative of "gates" in this interpretation is by omission of the particle "ka" (like). It is also said: the estimate is "and it becomes possessing gates," because all of it will become gates. It is also said: its gates are its paths. It is also said: it will dissolve and scatter until gates appear in it. It is also said: every servant has two gates in the heaven: a gate for his deeds and a gate for his provision, and when the Resurrection comes, the gates will be opened.

In the hadith of the Night Journey: "Then we were taken up to the heaven, and Jibril asked for it to be opened. It was said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad.' It was said: 'Has he been sent for?' He said: 'He has been sent for.' So it was opened for us."

﴿And the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾, meaning they become nothing, just as a mirage: the onlooker thinks it is water, and it is not water. It is also said: they are set in motion, meaning they are uprooted from their foundations. It is also said: they are removed from their places.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾.
