Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾**: *mirṣād* is on the pattern *mif'āl* from *al-rasd* (watching, lying in wait). *Al-rasd* is anything that is in front of you. Al-Hasan said: "Over the Fire there is a watch. No one enters Paradise until he has crossed over it. Whoever comes with a passport (*jawāz*) passes, and whoever does not come with a passport is detained." It is narrated from Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Over it there are three bridges." It was also said: *mirṣādan* means "possessing watchposts" by way of *nisba* (attribution), that is, it watches over those who pass by it. Muqatil said: "a place of detention." It was also said: "a road and a passage, so there is no way to Paradise until one crosses Hell." In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: "*al-mirṣād* is the path." Al-Qushayri mentioned that *al-mirṣād* is the place where the single person watches for the enemy, like *al-miḍmār*, the place where horses are trained (*tuḍmar*), that is, it is prepared for them. So *al-mirṣād* means the place. The angels watch the disbelievers until they descend into Hell. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Abu Sinan (in one manuscript: Abu Sufyan) that it means *rāṣida* (watching), who requites them for their deeds. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: "*al-rāṣid* of a thing is the one who observes it. You say: *rasadahu yarṣuduhu rasdan wa rasadan*, and *al-tarassud* is *al-taraqqub* (watching closely). *Al-marṣad* is the place of watching." Al-Asma'i said: "*rasadtuhu arṣuduhu*: I watched him closely, and *arṣadtuhu*: I prepared for him." Al-Kisa'i said the same. I say: Hell is therefore prepared and lying in wait (*mutaraṣṣida*), on the pattern *mutafa''il* from *al-rasad*, which is watching closely, that is, it is ever watchful for whoever comes. *Al-mirṣād* is *mif'āl*, one of the intensive patterns, like *al-mi'ṭār* and *al-mighyār*, so it is as if Hell is constantly awaiting the disbelievers.

**﴿For the transgressors, a destination﴾**: this is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *mirṣādan*. *Al-ma'āb* is the return place, that is, a place to which they return. It is said: *āba yaʾūbu awbatan*, when he returned. Qatadah said: "a refuge and an abode." By "the transgressors" is meant those who transgress in their religion by disbelief, or in their worldly life by wrongdoing.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾**: that is, they will remain in the Fire as long as the ages (*al-aḥqāb*) last, and these do not end; whenever one age passes, another age comes. *Al-ḥuqub*, with two *ḍammas*, means a long period of time, and *al-aḥqāb* means periods of time. *Al-ḥiqbah*, with a *kasra*, means a year, and its plural is *ḥiqab*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Tamimi said:

*"We were like the two drinking companions of Judhayma for an age of time, until it was said that they would never part.*
*When we separated, it was as if I and Malik, because of the long time we had been together, had never spent a single night together."*

*Al-ḥuqb*, with a *ḍamma* and a *sukūn*, is eighty years. It was also said to be more or less than that, as will come. Its plural is *aḥqāb*. The meaning in the verse is: *lābithīna fīhā aḥqāba al-ākhira* (remaining therein for the ages of the Hereafter), which have no end. The word *al-ākhira* is omitted because the context indicates it, since the mention of the Hereafter is in the speech; it is like saying *ayyām al-ākhira* (the days of the Hereafter), meaning days after days without end. It would indicate a fixed time only if He had said "five ages" or "ten ages" or the like. The ages are mentioned because the age was the furthest thing in their estimation, so He spoke in terms that their imaginations reach and that they understand. It is a metaphor for eternity, that is, they remain in it forever. It was also said: the ages were mentioned rather than days, because ages are more terrifying to hearts and more indicative of eternity. The meanings are close. This eternal abiding applies to the polytheists. It is possible to apply the verse to the sinners who will leave the Fire after ages. It was also said: the ages are a period in which they drink *al-ḥamīm* and *al-ghassāq*, and when these are over they will have another kind of punishment; for this reason He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ **﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾**.

*Lābithīn* is the active participle of *labitha*. This is strengthened by the fact that its verbal noun is *al-lubth* with a *sukūn*, like *al-shurb*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lābithīna* without an *alif*, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. Both are dialects: it is said *rajulun lābithun* and *labith*, like *ṭamia* and *ṭāmi'*, and *fariha* and *fārih*. It is also said: *huwa labithun bi-makān kadhā*, meaning that remaining there has become his condition; it is likened to what is natural in a person, like *ḥadhir* and *faraq*, because the pattern *fa'il* is mostly for what is natural in a thing, whereas the active participle of *lābith* is not so.

*Al-ḥuqb* is eighty years according to Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu Hurayra. A year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn 'Umar narrated this as a *marfū'* report from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayra said: "A year is three hundred and sixty days, each day like the days of this world." It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "*al-ḥuqb* is forty years." al-Suddi: seventy years. It was also said: it is a thousand months, narrated by Abu Umama as a *marfū'* report. Bashir ibn Ka'b: three hundred years. Al-Hasan: "None of you knows what the ages are, but it has been mentioned that they are a hundred *ḥuqb*, and each *ḥuqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count." Also from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Each *ḥuqb* is thirty thousand years." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and the first (report) by al-Mawardi. Qutrub said: it is a long, undefined period. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, no one who enters the Fire will leave it until he has remained in it for ages. The *ḥuqb* is some eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count. So let none of you rely on the hope that he will leave the Fire." Al-Tha'labi mentioned this. Al-Qurazi said: the ages are forty-three *ḥuqb*, each *ḥuqb* is seventy autumns, each autumn is seven hundred years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years.

I say: these are contradictory statements. The limitation in the verse is for eternity, and it needs an authoritative transmission that cuts off excuses, and this has not been established from the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning, Allah knows best, is what we mentioned at first: they remain therein for periods and eras, whenever one period passes another follows it, and an era follows another era, thus forever, without cessation. Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is that they have no end in terms of termination, as if He had said "forever." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it is abrogated (*mansūkha*) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So taste; We will increase you only in punishment﴾, meaning that the counting has ended and eternity has been achieved. I say: this is far-fetched, because it is a report, and He has said, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], as was mentioned before. This applies to the disbelievers. As for the sinful monotheists, the statement is correct, and "abrogation" here means "specification." Allah knows best.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is "in the earth," since it has already been mentioned, and the pronoun in ﴿they will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ refers to Hell.

It was also said: the singular of *al-aḥqāb* is *ḥuqb* and *ḥiqba*. He said:

*"If you are away from her for a ḥiqba, you will not meet her, so you are as one who has tried by what you have done."*

Al-Kumayt said: *"And no camel-litters passed, nor encampments—*
*He passed by her after an age, an age."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they will not taste therein﴾, that is, in the ages, ﴿coolness﴾ **﴿nor drink﴾**. *Al-bard* means sleep according to Abu 'Ubayda and others. A poet said:

*"Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and if I wished I would not taste sweet water nor sleep."*

This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi, and they cited al-Kindi's verse:

*"Its sips grew cool on me, so sleep (al-bard) turned me away from it and from kissing it."*

That is, sleep. The Arabs say: *manaʿa al-bard al-bard*, meaning: the coolness removed sleep. I say: a hadith has come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether there is sleep in Paradise. He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Likewise the Fire, and Allah, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-bard* is the coolness of drink. He also said: *al-bard* is sleep, and *al-sharāb* is water. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning they will not taste the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep. He made *al-bard* the coolness of everything that brings comfort. This is a coolness that benefits them; as for *al-zamharīr* (the freezing cold), it is a cold by which they are harmed, so it does not benefit them, and they have from it of punishment what Allah alone knows. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *bardan* means refreshment and rest. A poet said, the speaker being Humayd ibn Thawr describing a tree and by it referring to a woman:

*"The shade does not endure the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the shadow of the afternoon, at the times of evening, taste ..."*

﴿They will not taste therein coolness nor drink﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the transgressors, or a qualifier of the ages. So "the ages" is a time adverb, and what governs it is *lābithīna*, or *lābithīna* in the sense of transitivity of *fa'ila*.

﴿except scalding water and ghassāq﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnā' munqaṭi'*) according to those who take *al-bard* to be sleep. Whoever takes it as coldness makes this a substitute for it. *Al-ḥamīm* is hot water, according to Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ḥamīm* is the tears of their eyes, gathered in pools and then given to them to drink. Al-Nahhas said: the root of *al-ḥamīm* is hot water, and from it is derived *al-ḥammām* (bath), and from it *al-ḥumma* (fever), and from it ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾; it is meant only to indicate the extreme of heat. *Al-ghassāq* is the pus and the discharge of the people of the Fire. It was also said to be *al-zamharīr*. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a shadda on the *sīn*, and the discussion of it has already passed in (the commentary on) *Ṣād*.

﴿A fitting recompense﴾: that is, corresponding to their deeds, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. So *al-wifāq* means *al-muwāfaqa* (correspondence), like *al-qitāl* meaning *al-muqātala*. *Jazā'an* is in the accusative as an infinitive, that is, "We requited them with a recompense that corresponded to their deeds," as al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said. Al-Farra' also said: it is the plural of *al-wafq*, and *al-wafq* and *al-lafq* are one. Muqatil said: the punishment corresponded to the sin, for there is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought upon them what would grieve them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾, that is, they did not fear an accounting for their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning. Al-Zajjaj: that is, they did not believe in the Resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning.

﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial (kiḍḍāban)﴾: that is, with what the prophets brought. It was also said: with what We revealed of the Books. The reading of the majority is *kiddāban*, with a shadda on the *dhāl* and a *kasra* on the *kāf*, from *kadhdhaba*, meaning they denied with great denial. Al-Farra' said: it is a broad Yemeni dialect; they say *kadhdhabtu [bihi] kiddāban* (the addition is from al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*), and *kharraqtu al-qamīṣa kharrāqan* (I tore the shirt), and every verb on the pattern *fa''ala* has as its verbal noun *fi''āl* with a shadda in their dialect. One of the Kilab poets recited:

*"Indeed, how long you have held me back from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from our healing."*

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read *kidhāban* without a shadda, and this is also a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali said: both the light and the heavy forms are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual lying), like the saying of al-A'sha:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying."*

Abu al-Fath said: both came as verbal nouns of *kadhaba* and *kadhdhaba*. Al-Zamakhshari said: *kidhāban* with a light *dhāl* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, as evidenced by his saying:

*"So I believed her and I disbelieved her ... and a man is benefited by his lying (kadhābah)."*

This is like His saying: ﴿He caused you to grow out of the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh 71:17], meaning: ﴿And they denied Our signs with a denial﴾, ﴿so they lied a lie﴾. Or you may take it as an object of *kadhdhabu* (they denied), because it implies the meaning *kadhabu* (they lied), since everyone who denies the truth is a liar. When they regard the Muslims as liars, and the Muslims regard them as liars, there is mutual lying (*mukadhaba*) between them.

Ibn 'Umar read *kuffaban* (with a *damma* on the *kaf* and a *shadda*), the plural of *kadhib* (liar). Abu Hatim reported this. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The word *al-kuddhab* may also mean the one who is extremely effective in lying. One says *rajul kuddhab* (a man who is a great liar), like your saying *hussan* (a great beautiful one) and *bukhkhal* (a great miser). In this case it is an adjective of the verbal noun in *kadhdhabu*, meaning a denial of an extremely lying kind, whose lying is excessive.

In *al-Sihah* (a lexicon by al-Jawhari) it says: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied Our signs with a denial﴾ (*kiddhaban*) is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come in the pattern *taf'il* like *al-taklim* (speaking), in the pattern *fi'al* like *kiddhab*, in the pattern *taf'ila* like *tawsiya* (instruction), and in the pattern *mufa''al*, as in ﴿and We tore them completely apart﴾ (*mazzaqnahum kulla mumazzaq*) [Saba' 34:19].

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record﴾. *Kulla* is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by *ahsaynahu* (We enumerated it), meaning: and We enumerated everything, We enumerated it. Abu al-Sammal read *wa-kullu shay'* (with *kullu* in the nominative) as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Kitaban* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, because the meaning of *ahsayna* is *katabna* (We wrote), meaning: We wrote it as a writing.

It was then said that by this he meant knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. It was also said: meaning, We wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*, the tablet on which the divine decree is recorded) so that the angels would know it. And it was said: he meant what was written against the servants of their deeds. This writing came from the angels assigned to the servants, by the command of God, exalted is He, to them to write, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and writing, they know whatever you do﴾ [al-Infitar 82:10–11].

﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. Abu Barzah said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the most severe verse in the Qur'an. He said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾. That is, ﴿every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:56], and ﴿every time it dies down, We increase them in the blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 17:97].

**The Qur'an commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 78, verses 31–36:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of attainment﴾. He mentioned the reward of those who avoid disobeying the command of God. *Mafaza* (a place of attainment) means a place of success, deliverance and release from what the people of the Fire are in. For this reason the desert whose water is scarce is called *mafazah*, out of optimism (*tafa'ul*) about being delivered from it.

(﴿Gardens and grapevines﴾) This is an explanation of *al-fawz* (attainment). It is also said that the meaning of ﴿for the righteous there is a place of attainment﴾ is: indeed, for the righteous there are gardens. *Hada'iq* is the plural of *hadiqah*, which is an enclosed orchard, and it is said *ahdaqa bihi*, meaning "it surrounded him." *Al-a'nab* is the plural of *inab* (grapes), meaning vineyards of grapes, and the word (vineyards) has been omitted.

(﴿And full-breasted maidens of equal age﴾) *Kawa'ib* is the plural of *ka'ib*, which means a girl whose breasts have swelled (*nahid*). It is said: *ka'abat al-jariyah yak'ubu ku'uban* and *ka'abat yuka'{\i}bu takeeban*, and *nahadat yanhadu nuhudan*. Al-Dahhak said: "like the full-breasted young women." From this is the saying of Qays ibn 'Asim:

*"How many a chaste, noble woman we have possessed, and of full-breasted maidens who did not know what hardship is, one who has reached puberty."*

*Al-atrab* means peers in age. This has been discussed in Surah "al-Waqi'ah" [[See vol. 17, p. 211]]. Its singular is *tirb*.

(﴿And a full cup﴾) Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas said: *mutra'ah*, meaning filled to the brim. It is said: *adhhaqtu al-ka's*, meaning I filled the cup, and *ka's dihaq* means a full cup. He said:

*"Ah, give me to drink pure wine, which the cupbearer has poured for me from its water in your full cup."*

Khidash ibn Zuhayr said:

*"Amir came to us seeking our hospitality, so we filled for him a full cup."*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas also said: *mutatabi'ah*, meaning successive, one following another. From this comes *idhdahaqat al-hijarah idhdihaqan*, which means the tight fitting of the stones and the entering of some of them into others. So the successive is like the interlocking. It is also reported from 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn Aslam: *safiyah*, meaning pure. The poet said:

*"You are closer to the heart in nearness than the thirsty one is to a full cup."*

It is the plural of *dahaq*, and in *Lisan al-'Arab* (under *dahaq*): "*al-dahaq* (with a vowel on the first letter) is a kind of torture; it is in Persian *ishkinjah*. *Dahaqtu al-shay'* means I broke and cut it." [[The reading in Lisan is as quoted; the source has "a kind of torture"]] The word refers to two pieces of wood by which the shin is squeezed, [[The correction is from lexicon books; the original reads: two pieces of wood that are squeezed]] and it is by these two that the leg is pressed.

The meaning of *al-ka's* here is wine, so the sense is: wine having *dihaq*, that is, pressed and purified. This was said by al-Qushayri. In *al-Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): "*Adhhaqtu al-ma'*" means I poured out the water with great force. Abu 'Amr said: "*al-dahaq*, with a vowel on the first letter, is a kind of torture; in Persian it is *ashkinjah*." Al-Mubarrad said: "*al-madhuq* is one tormented with every torment with no relief from it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "*dahaqtu al-shay'*" means I broke it and cut it, and likewise *dahdaqtuhu*. He recited for Hujr ibn Khalid:

*"We crush pieces of meat for the sweet and the sound (?), and some of them boil in cooking pots (maneq) of blame."* [[This is narrated so in Lisan under the root dahaq. In the originals it reads "cooking pots"; the maneq are small pots, singular mutqa'/minqah.]]

*Dahmaqtuhu* with an added *mim* has the same meaning. Al-Asma'i said: *al-dahmaqah* is the softness, sweetness and delicacy of food, and likewise everything soft. From it is the hadith of 'Umar: "If I wished that it be made soft for me, I would have done it, but God criticised a people when He said: ﴿You used up your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 20]."

﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, ﴿any vain talk or lying﴾. *Al-laghw* is falsehood, which is what is discarded and thrown away from speech. From it is the hadith: "If you say to your companion 'Be silent' on Friday while the imam is delivering the sermon, you have engaged in *laghw*." [[That is because the people of Paradise, when they drink, their minds are not altered, and they do not speak vain talk, unlike the people of this world.]] As for ﴿nor lying﴾, it has been mentioned before, meaning that some of them do not call others liars, and they do not hear falsehood. Al-Kisa'i read *kiddaban* with a light pronunciation from *kadhabtu kidhaban*, meaning they do not lie to each other in Paradise. It is also said: both are verbal nouns of "denial" (*takdhib*), but he lightened it here because it is not restricted to a verb from which it becomes a verbal noun. The word in His saying ﴿and they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾ is pronounced with doubled *dhal*, because *kadhdhabu* restricts the verbal noun to *kidhdhab* (intense denial).

﴿A reward from your Lord﴾: the accusative here is as a verbal noun, because the meaning is: He rewarded them for what has been mentioned, a reward (*jaza'*), and likewise ﴿a gift﴾ (*'ata'*), because "He gave them" and "He rewarded them" have one meaning, that is, He gave them a gift. ﴿Sufficient﴾ (*hisaban*) means abundant, as said by Qatadah. It is said: *ahsabtu fulanan*, meaning I multiplied the gift for him until he said *hasbi* (enough for me). A woman of the Banu Qushayr said [[The one who said it was a woman of the Banu Qushayr. *Nuqfi* means: we give to him the *qifyah*, which is what is given to the guest and the child.]]:

*"We give to the young child of the tribe if he is hungry, and we give him enough (ahsabu) even if he is not hungry."*

Al-Qutabi said: "We see the origin of this to be that one gives him until he says *hasbi*." Al-Zajjaj said: *hisaban* means what suffices them. Al-Akhfash said the same. It is said: *ahsabuni kadha*, meaning it sufficed me. Al-Kalbi said: "He calculated with them and gave them ten times for each good deed." Mujahid said: "*hisaban* for what they did," so *al-hisab* here means counting, that is, according to what was due to them in the promise of the Lord. He promised ten times for a good deed, and He promised seven hundred times to some people, and He has promised some people a reward that has no end and no measure, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10].

Abu Hashim recited *'ata'an hisaban* with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and a doubled *sin*, on the pattern of *fa''al*, meaning *kafafan* (sufficient). Al-Asma'i said: "The Arabs say: *hassabtu al-rajul* with doubling, when I honoured him." He recited the poet's line:

*"When his guest comes to him, he honours him (yuhassibuh)."*

Ibn 'Abbas recited *hisanan* with the letter *nun* [[Al-Shawkani wrote the word this way in his tafsir Fath al-Qadir (5/258) without vowelling it.]].

**The Qur'an commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 78, verses 31–36:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of attainment﴾. He mentioned the reward of those who avoid disobeying the command of God. *Mafaza* (a place of attainment) means a place of success, deliverance and release from what the people of the Fire are in. For this reason the desert whose water is scarce is called *mafazah*, out of optimism (*tafa'ul*) about being delivered from it.

From it is the hadith of 'Umar: "If I wished that it be made soft for me, I would have done it, but God criticised a people when He said: ﴿You used up your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 20]."

﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, ﴿any vain talk or lying﴾. *Al-laghw* is falsehood, which is what is discarded and thrown away from speech. From it is the hadith: "If you say to your companion 'Be silent' on Friday while the imam is delivering the sermon, you have engaged in *laghw*." [[That is because the people of Paradise, when they drink, their minds are not altered, and they do not speak vain talk, unlike the people of this world.]] As for ﴿nor lying﴾, it has been mentioned before, meaning that some of them do not call others liars, and they do not hear falsehood. Al-Kisa'i read *kiddaban* with a light pronunciation from *kadhabtu kidhaban*, meaning they do not lie to each other in Paradise. It is also said: both are verbal nouns of "denial" (*takdhib*), but he lightened it here because it is not restricted to a verb from which it becomes a verbal noun. The word in His saying ﴿and they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾ is pronounced with doubled *dhal*, because *kadhdhabu* restricts the verbal noun to *kidhdhab* (intense denial).

﴿A reward from your Lord﴾: the accusative here is as a verbal noun, because the meaning is: He rewarded them for what has been mentioned, a reward (*jaza'*), and likewise ﴿a gift﴾ (*'ata'*), because "He gave them" and "He rewarded them" have one meaning, that is, He gave them a gift. ﴿Sufficient﴾ (*hisaban*) means abundant, as said by Qatadah. It is said: *ahsabtu fulanan*, meaning I multiplied the gift for him until he said *hasbi* (enough for me). A woman of the Banu Qushayr said [[The one who said it was a woman of the Banu Qushayr. *Nuqfi* means: we give to him the *qifyah*, which is what is given to the guest and the child.]]:

*"We give to the young child of the tribe if he is hungry, and we give him enough (ahsabu) even if he is not hungry."*

Al-Qutabi said: "We see the origin of this to be that one gives him until he says *hasbi*." Al-Zajjaj said: *hisaban* means what suffices them. Al-Akhfash said the same. It is said: *ahsabuni kadha*, meaning it sufficed me. Al-Kalbi said: "He calculated with them and gave them ten times for each good deed." Mujahid said: "*hisaban* for what they did," so *al-hisab* here means counting, that is, according to what was due to them in the promise of the Lord. He promised ten times for a good deed, and He promised seven hundred times to some people, and He has promised some people a reward that has no end and no measure, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10].

Abu Hashim recited *'ata'an hisaban* with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and a doubled *sin*, on the pattern of *fa''al*, meaning *kafafan* (sufficient). Al-Asma'i said: "The Arabs say: *hassabtu al-rajul* with doubling, when I honoured him." He recited the poet's line:

*"When his guest comes to him, he honours him (yuhassibuh)."*

Ibn 'Abbas recited *hisanan* with the letter *nun* [[Al-Shawkani wrote the word this way in his tafsir Fath al-Qadir (5/258) without vowelling it.]].

**The Qur'an commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 78, verses 31–36:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of attainment﴾. He mentioned the reward of those who avoid disobeying the command of God. *Mafaza* (a place of attainment) means a place of success, deliverance and release from what the people of the Fire are in. For this reason the desert whose water is scarce is called *mafazah*, out of optimism (*tafa'ul*) about being delivered from it.

(﴿Gardens and grapevines﴾) This is an explanation of *al-fawz* (attainment). It is also said that the meaning of ﴿for the righteous there is a place of attainment﴾ is: indeed, for the righteous there are gardens. *Hada'iq* is the plural of *hadiqah*, which is an enclosed orchard, and it is said *ahdaqa bihi*, meaning "it surrounded him." *Al-a'nab* is the plural of *inab* (grapes), meaning vineyards of grapes, and the word (vineyards) has been omitted.

(﴿And full-breasted maidens of equal age﴾) *Kawa'ib* is the plural of *ka'ib*, which means a girl whose breasts have swelled (*nahid*). It is said: *ka'abat al-jariyah yak'ubu ku'uban* and *ka'abat yuka'{\i}bu takeeban*, and *nahadat yanhadu nuhudan*. Al-Dahhak said: "like the full-breasted young women." From this is the saying of Qays ibn 'Asim:

*"How many a chaste, noble woman we have possessed, and of full-breasted maidens who did not know what hardship is, one who has reached puberty."*

*Al-atrab* means peers in age. This has been discussed in Surah "al-Waqi'ah" [[See vol. 17, p. 211]]. Its singular is *tirb*.

(﴿And a full cup﴾) Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas said: *mutra'ah*, meaning filled to the brim. It is said: *adhhaqtu al-ka's*, meaning I filled the cup, and *ka's dihaq* means a full cup. He said:

*"Ah, give me to drink pure wine, which the cupbearer has poured for me from its water in your full cup."*

Khidash ibn Zuhayr said:

*"Amir came to us seeking our hospitality, so we filled for him a full cup."*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas also said: *mutatabi'ah*, meaning successive, one following another. From this comes *idhdahaqat al-hijarah idhdihaqan*, which means the tight fitting of the stones and the entering of some of them into others. So the successive is like the interlocking. It is also reported from 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn Aslam: *safiyah*, meaning pure. The poet said:

*"You are closer to the heart in nearness than the thirsty one is to a full cup."*

It is the plural of *dahaq*, and in *Lisan al-'Arab* (under *dahaq*): "*al-dahaq* (with a vowel on the first letter) is a kind of torture; it is in Persian *ishkinjah*. *Dahaqtu al-shay'* means I broke and cut it." In *al-Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): "*Adhhaqtu al-ma'*" means I poured out the water with great force. Abu 'Amr said: "*al-dahaq*, with a vowel on the first letter, is a kind of torture; in Persian it is *ashkinjah*." Al-Mubarrad said: "*al-madhuq* is one tormented with every torment with no relief from it." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "*dahaqtu al-shay'*" means I broke it and cut it, and likewise *dahdaqtuhu*.
